scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The polka-mazurka originated in the 1850s, with Johann Strauss II's 'La Viennoise' (1854) cited as the first example by the Strauss family.
It was widely adopted in European salons as a cross-cultural variant of the polka, influenced by the French-polka and the schnell-polka.
on_screen: Map: Austria · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It was a social ballroom dance, valued for its elegance and ability to express romantic sentiment.
It was often performed in public and private social gatherings.
Today it is a historical tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in 3/4 time, with a step sequence spanning two measures (six counts).
It involves a glide to the second position, a draw to the first, and a hop, with the lady mirroring the cavalier's movements in reverse.
It is typically danced in a waltz-like rotation or in a straight line.
Watch for Polka-Mazurka Step.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Couples dance in rotation or straight lines.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is written in 3/4 time, emphasizing the first beat of the bar.
It typically features a main theme followed by a subsidiary theme and a free-style 'trio' section.
The pulse is 3/4.
A 3/4 time signature piece that avoids unequal note values, ensuring a clear, consistent triple-beat pulse that feels more deliberate than a waltz.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Johann Strauss II, Josef Strauss, and Eduard Strauss are the most prominent composers associated with the genre.
The dance shares characteristics with the Polish mazurka and the Nordic polska, though it remains distinct in its specific step-combination and ballroom application.
It is a hybrid form, subclassed under both the polka and the mazurka, with influences from the French-polka and the schnell-polka.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: polka-mazurka is parent of Polka: The polka-mazurka derives its movement style and name from the polka.
polka-mazurka is parent of Mazurka: The polka-mazurka derives its 3/4 musical structure from the mazurka.
polka-mazurka is sibling of Redowa: Often taught alongside the polka-mazurka in 19th-century dance manuals.
